title: Serving Runtime Reference: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling, and Ops Playbook
author: Ava Chen
summary: Comprehensive reference covering the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling model, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks used by the Serving Runtime team.
body:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference's Serving Runtime: runtime architecture, kernel & scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on serving-runtime, infra, SRE, and applied ML who operate or extend runtime components.

Table of contents
1. Runtime architecture (high level)
2. Kernel & scheduling model
3. Profiling & profiling-playbook (how-to)
4. Benchmarking suite and CI integration
5. Release notes (last three releases)
6. Known issues and mitigations
7. Runbooks: incident triage and common procedures
8. Team wiki pointers and ownership

1. Runtime architecture (high level)

Short summary: The serving runtime is composed of a control plane (orchestrator, admission, routing), a hosting layer (worker pool managers), and a GPU-optimized inference engine (inference-service). Key goals: predictable P99 latency targets, throughput elasticity, and safe fallbacks.

Core services and responsibilities:
- inference-service: Tensor/attention execution, KV cache management, quantized kernels. (Owned by serving-runtime/backend).
- request-router: policy-based routing (latency/cost/region/customer-tier). (Owned by serving-runtime/controller).
- batch-coordinator: performs micro-batching and continuous batching.
- cache-service: prefix and KV caching, hot-shard replication.
- autoscaler: scales GPU pools based on QPS, cold start profiles, and SLO headroom.
- control-plane-api: model versions, rollout config, and telemetry hooks.

SLOs and thresholds (current):
- Hosted inference P99 (<= 300ms for small models, <= 1200ms for long-seq L>=2048)
- P95 tail SLO: 95% requests within target by model-class
- Error budget per service: 0.1% monthly for inference-service
- CPU throttling threshold: node CPU > 75% triggers autoscaler cooldown

Deployment topology:
- Multi-az clusters with cross-zone capacity; smart-routing prefers local AZ but falls back to regional pool on capacity pressure.
- Dedicated pools (customer-dedicated) keep private routing tables and stricter fallbacks (no external region).

2. Kernel & scheduling model

Design goals: choose kernels per model type and sequence length, minimize device-to-device syncs, and preserve low-latency by avoiding unnecessary batching for single-token completion workloads.

Kernel selection rules:
- Kernel profiles indexed by (architecture, dtype, quantization, seq_len_bucket). The kernel selector chooses the lowest-cost kernel that meets latency constraints.
- Example mapping: transformer_xl/float16/seq<=128 -> fused_attention_v3; seq>128 -> attention_shard_kernel_v2.

Scheduling primitives:
- Request priority: realtime (interactive), bulk (embeddings, batch jobs), background (cache warmers).
- Micro-batching window: 2–8 ms for realtime classes (configurable per model).
- KV cache pinning for cached prefixes: pinned allocations are placed on local GPU memory and accounted separately to avoid OOM during bursts.

Preemption & safe fallback:
- When a higher-priority request cannot be scheduled, batch-coordinator will: 1) attempt preemptive commit of non-critical micro-batches, 2) if unsuccessful, route to a lower-capacity fallback model (model-variant) or different region per routing policy.

3. Profiling & profiling-playbook (how-to)

Purpose: capture meaningful traces to diagnose latency regressions and kernel inefficiencies. Follow this playbook during triage or before a release.

A. Tools and collection points:
- perf-trace: kernel-level traces with timestamps (GPU + host).
- katana-profiler: end-to-end request traces (ingest -> router -> inference-service).
- dmetrics: aggregated histograms (p50/p95/p99, cpu/gpu memory, kernel time).

B. Standard profiling steps (triage):
1. Reproduce: use the benchmark harness to replay a failing request set (see section 4).
2. Collect: enable katana-profiler for the target pool for a 10-minute window.
   - Command: ```rbxctl trace start --pool serving-prod-eu --duration 10m --tags regression-2026-03```
3. Kernel trace: pull perf-trace for affected GPUs.
   - Command: ```perf-trace --gpu 0 --out /tmp/gpu-trace.pb```
4. Analyze: run analyzer (katana-analyze) to produce waterfall and kernel timing breakdown.
   - Example: ```katana-analyze /tmp/trace.pb --report /tmp/regression-report.html```
5. Action: if kernel contention > 60% of p99, escalate to kernel-team; if memory fragmentation is > 30%, open a task to improve allocator.

C. Profiling tips:
- Use pinned test clients to avoid client-side jitter during measurements.
- For intermittent tails, capture longer windows (>= 30 min) and correlate with autoscaler events.

4. Benchmarking suite and CI integration

Benchmark goals: validate end-to-end latency, kernel-level throughput, memory pressure, and scaling characteristics. Bench harness components:
- bench-harness: runner that replays recorded traces with configurable QPS, concurrency, and sequence length distributions.
- microbench: kernel-only runner (per-kernel throughput).
- e2e-smoke: lightweight test for CI verifying basic correctness and latency P95 within threshold.

CI gates:
- PR gate: e2e-smoke must pass on current-serving-image.
- Merge gate: full bench-harness run (reduced sample) for major kernel or scheduler changes.
- Nightly: full benchmark matrix across models and quant profiles (runs on dedicated bench cluster).

Example runner command:
```bash
bench-harness --model gpt-small-q4 --qps 250 --seq-dist short:0.6,mid:0.3,long:0.1 --duration 10m --report /artifacts/report.json
```
Bench metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, kernel-time breakdown, batch-size distribution, failed requests.

5. Release notes (high-level)

2026-03-01 (v2026.03.01) - Stable
- Kernel selector: added seq_len_bucket for fused_attention_v3 -> improved P99 by 12% for seq<=128 on A100 clusters.
- Autoscaler: cooldown tuning to reduce oscillations during burst loads.
- Fixed: memory fragmentation in cache-service that caused OOMs under sustained heavy cache write workloads.

2026-02-10 (v2026.02.10) - Patch
- Fix: continuous-batching race that could drop requests under extreme QPS.
- Perf: micro-batching window default reduced from 6ms -> 4ms for realtime classes.

2026-01-20 (v2026.01.20) - Major
- New: quantized kernel pipeline (q4/q8) with auto-fallback to float16 on accuracy regressions.
- New: bench-harness integration with CI nightly jobs.

6. Known issues and mitigations

Issue K-101: occasional p99 spikes for long-seq workloads during autoscaler events
- Symptoms: p99 increases by 2–3x for ~30–90s during horizontal scaling.
- Root cause: cold GPU warmup + kernel JIT compilation on first use.
- Mitigation: pre-warm kernels on scale-up (preload model artifacts, run priming runs). Use: ```rbxctl prewarm --pool serving-prod-us --model gpt-long```
- Long-term: kernel caching persistence (in progress, ETA Q2 2026).

Issue K-117: cache-service fragmentation after frequent small writes
- Symptoms: increased OOMs on smaller GPUs (40GB).
- Mitigation: trigger defragmentation job and evict low-use prefixes.
   - Command: ```cachectl defrag --pool serving-prod-eu --threshold 0.3```

Issue K-132: regression after quant pipeline change on some models
- Symptoms: small accuracy drift on classification tasks.
- Mitigation: automatic rollback to float16 variant and open regression triage.

7. Runbooks: incident triage and common procedures

A. P99 latency regression (step-by-step)
1. Verify: Check dashboards (serving-runtime/p99) and filter by model and pool.
2. Scope: is regression global, pool-level, or model-level?
3. Capture traces: follow profiling-playbook (Section 3).
4. If kernel-level: escalate to kernel-team with perf traces (label: kernel-urgent).
5. If autoscaler correlation: check autoscaler logs and recent scale events. Rollback if new release correlates.
6. Mitigate: reroute traffic to fallback model-variant or region.
   - Command: ```control-plane route update --model-id mdl_xyz --variant fallback-v1 --weight 100```

B. OOM on GPU (hot)
1. Identify process: ssh into node using incident user (ops@redwood).
2. Run: ```nvidia-smi topo --verbose && pmap -x <pid>```
3. If cache pressure: evict prefixes for customer or restart cache-service on node.
4. If allocator fragmentation: run defrag job (see known issues).
